LOS ANGELES, California (CNN)  -- It was a night for neon pink bow ties and words like "disaster" and "monstrosity." It was not the night, however, to be Paris Hilton, Mike Myers or Uwe Boll. Paula Einstein, Rebecca Marcotte and Kelie McIver do a parody of "Dancing Queen" to open the show. The 29th Annual Golden Raspberry Awards honored the worst film achievements of the year in a small theater in Hollywood on February 21. The night opened with a parody of the "Mamma Mia" song, "Dancing Queen," and ended with "Love Guru" being named worst picture. "It wasn't just the economy that tanked, so did the qualities of the movies being offered," Razzie founder John Wilson told CNN several weeks before the show. "I would suggest putting away all sharp [instruments] before putting the DVDs in your machine." Paris Hilton and Mike Myers came out on top -- or bottom -- for the awards. Hilton earned both the worst actress and worst supporting actress awards for her roles in "Hottie & the Nottie" and "Repo: The Genetic Opera." She was also awarded worst screen couple for her on-screen time with her co-stars Christine Lakin and Joel David Moore. Razzie host Gretchen Enders said that "Hottie & the Nottie" was "a vanity production in the worst sense... Hilton, who served as executive producer, has no one to blame but herself." Hilton's film had a budget of $2 million but only earned about $27,000 at the box office. "Under Obama's new plan, they wouldn't even have to pay taxes," Wilson deadpanned. Myers added worst actor to the "Love Guru" worst picture and worst screenplay Razzies. To save anyone else from having to watch it, Wilson shredded a DVD copy of the film on stage. Parody films "Disaster Movie" and "Meet the Spartans," each nominated in five categories, came away empty-handed. However, that doesn't mean the Razzie foundation thinks they were worthwhile. "When you invest the kind of money that a mainstream, big-budget star film requires, you want some insurance that your investment is going to come back to you. So... you're going to do what worked before," Wilson said. "Financially that may make sense, but in terms of the audience's enjoyment, surprise or appreciation of what you're doing, it doesn't work." Enter "Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull," this year's winner of the worst prequel, remake, rip-off or sequel award. "A fourth installment of a beloved franchise, but this one found itself loved by almost no one," hosts Katsy Chappell and Josh Thoemke said. The approximately 740 voting members of the Raspberry Foundation also found Pierce Brosnan's singing voice sorely lacking. His role in "Mama Mia" earned him the worst supporting actor award. "An actor who could not sing, should not sing and arguably did not sing, in a role he should not have accepted," Razzie hosts Chip Dornell and Kelie McIver said about the former James Bond. But perhaps the biggest "winner" of the night was Uwe Boll. Recipient of the worst director award, the foundation also recognized his lifetime work with the worst career achievement award. Boll is the "worst living director on Earth," Wilson told CNN. Boll had a sense of humor about his Razzie success. He sent in a video rejection speech from a fake set of Darfur, Sudan, saying the Razzies had ruined his life and he would never be back. The Razzie team is already predicting next year's nominees. A few to watch out for: "Hannah Montana," "Friday the 13th" and "Bride Wars," -- the last of which has already grossed more than $50 million. "It's kind of like watching a train wreck, isn't it?" Wilson said.

# Los Angeles, California

Los Angeles, California, is one of the most iconic and culturally significant cities in the United States. Known widely by its abbreviation "LA," this sprawling metropolis serves as the second-most populous city in the country, trailing only New York City. Situated in Southern California along the Pacific coastline, Los Angeles is celebrated for its diverse population, thriving entertainment industry, and unique blend of urban and natural landscapes.

## Geography and Climate

Los Angeles spans a vast area, characterized by a mix of coastal beaches, urban neighborhoods, and mountainous terrain. The city enjoys a Mediterranean climate, with warm, dry summers and mild, wet winters. This favorable weather has long attracted residents and visitors alike, contributing to the city's reputation as a desirable place to live and work.

## Entertainment Capital of the World

Perhaps most famously, Los Angeles is home to Hollywood, the historic center of the American film and television industry. Major studios, production companies, and countless talented individuals in the entertainment field have made LA synonymous with movies, music, and celebrity culture. The Hollywood Sign, perched in the hills overlooking the city, stands as a global symbol of fame and aspiration.

## Cultural Diversity

Los Angeles boasts remarkable ethnic and cultural diversity, with communities representing nearly every corner of the globe. Neighborhoods such as Koreatown, Little Tokyo, and Boyle Heights reflect this rich tapestry, offering distinct culinary, artistic, and cultural experiences. This diversity has shaped LA's identity, making it a melting pot of traditions, languages, and cuisines.

## Economic Significance

Beyond entertainment, Los Angeles supports a robust economy driven by various industries, including technology, international trade, fashion, and tourism. The Port of Los Angeles is one of the busiest shipping ports in the nation, underscoring the city's role as a major hub for commerce and global trade within California and beyond.

## Conclusion

Los Angeles, California, continues to captivate people worldwide with its blend of natural beauty, cultural richness, and economic opportunity. Whether known for its film industry, diverse communities, or scenic coastline, LA remains a defining symbol of American culture and ambition.

## Worst Picture

The evening's marquee category typically goes to a film that either tried too hard or didn't try at all. Historical "winners" have included *Batman & Robin*, *Gigli*, and *Cats*—the last of which inspired co-host commentary along the lines of: "We've seen digital fur technology fail before, but never with such Broadway confidence."

This year's nominees followed the proud tradition of bloated franchise entries and vanity projects nobody asked for. As one presenter noted, "The Academy rewards films that move us. We reward films that make us check our phones."

## Worst Actor

The competition for Worst Actor remains fierce, as it requires a special kind of commitment to bad choices. Past recipients have included Jaden Smith for *After Earth* and various once-respected actors who apparently lost bets with their agents.

"Worst Actor isn't about lack of talent," one Razzie founder famously observed. "It's about talent aimed directly at the wrong target, fired with total confidence."

This year's winner reportedly accepted the news with good humor, joining a growing list of stars—including Sandra Bullock and Halle Berry—who've shown up in person to collect their Razzie, trophy in one hand, Oscar in the other from years past.

## Worst Actress

The Worst Actress category has occasionally sparked controversy, particularly the infamous 2010 nomination of 10-year-old Jackson-then-newcomer for *The Twilight Saga*, which many considered a step too far and led organizers to reconsider age limits.

This year's "honoree" delivered a performance described by one Razzie voter as "emotionally available to absolutely nothing happening on screen." The award presentation included the classic line: "We don't do this to be cruel. We do this because someone has to hold the mirror up, even when the reflection is this rough."

## Worst Director

Perhaps the most brutal category, Worst Director requires failing not just one performance but an entire film's vision. Past recipients include M. Night Shyamalan (a multiple-time honoree) and the directing team behind *Movie 43*.

This year's winner was praised—if that's the word—for "achieving a tonal consistency of confusion from frame one to the credits." The presenter added dryly, "Give him credit: most directors need help making a mess this cohesive."

## Closing Remarks

As the ceremony wrapped, one host offered the evening's closing philosophy: "The Oscars celebrate the best of what film can do. We celebrate the worst of what film did do, on purpose, with a budget, and someone's approval. That's not just failure—that's achievement."

The Razzies continue to serve their purpose: reminding Hollywood that for every triumph, there's a $200 million disaster starring someone who definitely should have known better.

---

*The Golden Raspberry Awards are presented annually, honoring—if that's the word—the worst that Hollywood has to offer. No trophies were harmed in the making of this report, mostly because they're spray-painted golf balls.*
